title.narrative: Kerk in Actie SRIJANA II Project

description.narrative: Returnees of seasonal migration to India, local youths

The first phase of the project SRIJANA; Creating opportunities for socio-economic well-being of Migrant Returnees in Western Nepal, has been concluded. This project was started as a pilot joint initiative between Kerk in Actie (KiA), Cordaid and local KiA partners – United Missions to Nepal (UMN) and International Nepal Fellowship (INF), two of the oldest and largest Christian organizations in Nepal operating in the country since the mid-60s. The first phase was implemented from 1st October 2020 and ended on 31st December 2023, i.e. for 3 years plus an extension of 3 months.
The first phase of the project targeted around 2,000 migrant returnees or young potential migrants of Thalara Rural Municipality of Bajhang district in Sudurpaschim (far west) province and Kankasunradi Rural Municipality of Jumla district in Karnali province, who returned home from across the open border with India at the peak of Covid19 pandemic during the first few months of 2020. Around 200-300 thousands of returnees who lost their jobs and had meagre resources to survive were forced to return back home from India in very dire circumstances and this was taken as a humanitarian crisis situation. In that context Kerk in Actie and Cordaid/ICCO Nepal office decided to undertake a joint initiative, together with KiA partners in Nepal, with an approach of linking humanitarian assistance to longer term development and with an overall aim of creating self-employment opportunities at home for these youths.
When the Covid19 pandemic started in late 2019, like everywhere else in the world, the situation was very chaotic to say the least. Nobody knew how the context would evolve in the coming years and the priority was to deal with the pandemic and save lives. Obviously for Indian authorities the priority was to provide assistance to Indian citizens. The Nepali labor migrants who generally work as laborers in informal sector or security guards in India had no choice but to leave their jobs and return home with whatever savings they had at that moment. The border security forces, who themselves were very poorly equipped to deal with the crisis, could do little to manage the massive exodus of people crossing the borders from either side, which further exacerbated the spread of the disease and suffering. Hundreds of thousands of Nepalese made very painful journeys and reached home in the higher hills and mountains of western Nepal. Some even lost their lives. The media was covered with such disturbing news each day. The returnees mostly had no money and had no idea what they would do at home to earn a living.
To support implementing partners in achieving the project expected outcomes and outputs
